tags.gist: Says the paper appropriately seeks a risk-proportionate, least-burdensome framework and names supervision, reversibility, traceability and team performance as relevant.
Supports oversight when AI diagnoses autonomously or its unverified output enters care, but wants that distinguished from private, non-final drafts for the interpreting radiologist.
Rather than a non-device declaration, requests a narrowly bounded premarket enforcement-discretion policy for radiologist-supervised generative pre-drafting functions.
States the requested policy: enforcement discretion for image-analysis functions producing private draft text for the interpreting specialist, with technical controls blocking earlier release.
Says output communicated to clinicians or patients, presented as an interpretation or used to direct care before specialist verification should stay under premarket oversight.
Would make the human-AI system in its workflow the performance unit, measuring both errors assistance introduces and errors a prompted radiologist catches.
Wants four auditable modifiers named: output disposition, persistence and reversibility, verifiability against source material, and whether specialist review is required architecturally.
Wants the competency framework to treat supervised operation as its own evidentiary stage, sitting between non-clinical testing and independent use.
Discloses its commercial interest and says regulation should follow actual intended use, user, source material, error route and safeguards, not a physician's mere presence.
Defines the pre-drafting category by auditable deployment conditions, and says any AI interpretation reaching a clinician or patient is a clinical communication whatever its label.
Notes the CDS exclusion does not cover image analysis, so such functions remain device software functions under the January 2026 guidance.
Frames the request as premarket enforcement discretion for a function of low risk whose unverified output cannot enter care before specialist verification.
Asks whether its added containment, supervision, validation and monitoring conditions warrant a distinct policy or streamlined pathway beyond existing assistive classifications.
Says FDA's preserved enforcement-discretion authority lets it create the category while retaining jurisdiction, avoiding a false choice between no regulation and autonomous-diagnostic burden.
Says the practice-of-medicine provision does not settle the software's status; the basis is the function's low-risk architecture with sequestered, reversible output.
Endorses evaluating the final configured function rather than the foundation model, since one model may serve research, drafting, decision support or autonomous diagnosis.
Says an upstream provider marketing a model for autonomous diagnosis cannot escape device duties, but status should not turn on latent capability alone.
Says fine-tuning is no reliable bright line for risk; treatment should follow the final function and architecture, with responsibilities assigned along the chain.
Argues a private draft differs in kind from unverifiable measurement devices, since the radiologist holds the source images and can check every statement.
Says human-in-the-loop carries no weight by itself; specialist review counts only with source access, time, freedom to reject, no dissemination and affirmative finalization.
Proposes a graduated structure, benchmarking only, supervised operation with enforced review, then independent use, so stage-three evidence is not the price of stage two.
Would grant enforcement discretion only when every listed condition holds, so a drafting aid cannot drift into an unreviewed reporting channel.
Requires the intended user to be a physician credentialed to interpret the examination independently, not patients, other clinicians or unsupervised trainees.
Requires the workflow to force complete source-image access before finalization and to block image-suppressed report signing.
Requires the draft to stay sequestered in the radiologist's workspace, outside the record, portals and messaging, with retained copies used only for audit and quality.
Bars any automatic finalization or clinical action, and any timer, default or batch process that turns non-editing into authorization.
Requires affirmative radiologist issuance with full ability to edit, delete, replace or reject, and an interface that makes blank-start easy.
Wants human-factors evaluation of whether timing, prominence and explanation design cause premature closure, testing error detection under realistic workload.
Wants local validation of the configured function on representative data by retrospective, shadow, blinded or paired methods, without presuming a randomized trial.
Wants clinically meaningful measures such as omissions, false additions, laterality errors, rejection and correction rates, and team sensitivity versus unaided workflow, not text similarity.
Wants deployers to monitor discrepancies, correction and rejection rates, drift by modality, scanner and subgroup, and failures, with thresholds triggering rollback or suspension.
Allows radiologist corrections to feed offline retraining, but a production model must not change behavior after each correction without validated, controlled deployment.
Wants records of model version, draft, edits, final report, timing and failures, with access control, cybersecurity and vendor-change notification proportionate to deployment.
Excludes from discretion any unverified output reaching clinicians or patients, and treats worklist prioritization as a separate function that does not disqualify a sequestered draft.
Says automation bias and anchoring should be measured against the real baseline of unaided interpretation, which itself suffers fatigue, satisfaction of search and serial dependence.
Wants the assisted workflow compared with realistic unaided practice, measuring errors introduced and prevented, sensitivity, completeness, time, fatigue effects and user variability.
Says a structured draft may reduce omissions, the commonest reporting error, and evaluation must capture errors prevented as well as introduced to support benefit-risk.
Lists human-factors safeguards: labelled unverified text, blank-report option, no passive acceptance, training, interface testing, separate tracking of AI-induced errors, periodic adjudication.
Makes human-AI team performance the principal unit for supervised drafting, asking whether the final report's accuracy, completeness, variability and timeliness hold up.
Makes downstream clinical reliance before specialist verification the regulatory boundary, contrasting the sequestered draft pathway with preliminary outputs reaching clinicians.
Calls local validation a safety layer, as imaging AI varies by site; wants institutions to validate, start in shadow mode and keep rollback.
Notes an IRB may be needed for research activities but is no general substitute for device regulation or everyday clinical AI governance.
Says specialist corrections yield valuable error data for offline retraining, but the production system should never learn silently; release only validated versions.
Calls sequestered supervised drafting a strong candidate for the trade, with monitoring as an added control conditioned on enforced sequestration, thresholds, auditability and rollback.
Allocates duties to the upstream model provider, downstream developer, deploying organization and interpreting radiologist, from version disclosure to independent image review.
Finds the voluntary master file concept, with the downstream sponsor staying responsible, more appropriate than treating every capable model as a finished diagnostic device.
Says that if premarket review is required, the evidence should stay proportionate to actual intended use, safeguards and residual risk.
Calls the axes useful but incomplete, adding traceability, user expertise, dissemination barriers, reversibility, time pressure, mandatory review, monitoring and uncontrolled change.
Illustrates with one model producing identical text: private in the radiologist's workspace versus sent to the emergency physician as a preliminary result.
Urges distinguishing architecturally enforced review, inspectable in configuration and logs, from advisory review that merely expects user behavior.
Would judge directiveness functionally by recipient, specificity, whether it enters records or ordering systems, and whether specialist verification must come first.
Says disclaimers cannot make directive output non-directive, but diagnostic language in a private, non-final draft does not make it action-directing.
Says unverified output delivered to patients is riskier, especially diagnoses or care instructions, but patient-facing status alone should not make a function high risk.
Says the pre-draft must be technically blocked from portals and inboxes, with patients receiving only the radiologist-issued report.
Treats specialist expertise as a risk modifier when paired with source access, exclusive finalization and training; status alone does not remove oversight.
Wants conversational risk assessed over whole trajectories with testing for migration toward directive output, hard scope boundaries and escalation.
Wants both escalation errors measured separately with context-specific criteria, weighing severity, prevalence, urgency and available review.
Calls the framework useful if it evaluates the configured workflow, confirming the radiologist-plus-draft process rather than the model as an autonomous diagnostician.
Refers back to its proposal of a supervised-operation stage between benchmarking and independent operation, with evidence calibrated per stage.
Would base evidence on residual risk after actual safeguards, rising as output moves toward direct delivery, action-directing behavior or autonomy.
Calls the structure a starting point and adds image-grounding tests for omissions, laterality, measurements, prior comparison and consistency, not text-similarity metrics.
For supervised drafting, wants correction, rejection, AI-induced and AI-corrected error rates measured, plus tests that drafts cannot be auto-finalized.
Proposes a fabricated-specificity element: measurements, comparisons or history asserted that cannot derive from the inputs, plausible yet invented.
Proposes measuring whether review functions via adoption rates, edit distances and blinded re-reads, cautioning against seeding errors into live drafts.
Treats benchmarks as predictive only when relevant, independent and representative, with sequestration, holdouts, locked configurations and adjudication; public sets are not superior.
Permits documented sponsor benchmarks where no public one fits, not as sole evidence, and accepts reasonable demonstrations of independence from upstream training data.
Lists confirmation methods for private drafting, says randomized trials should not be automatic, and reserves prospective evidence for outputs reaching clinicians or acting.
Wants prespecified endpoints and methods, reporting of intervals, reader and site variability and repeated runs, clustering accounted for, and no automatic pooling of synthetic data.
Finds synthetic data useful for stress tests and rare cases but no substitute for real imaging, with safeguards against reproducing a related model's blind spots.
Uses specialist panels or adjudicated references with criteria on clinically significant agreement; the team is the principal unit and device-alone results characterize failure modes.
Says the comparator should be the care likely without the device, for private drafting realistic unaided reporting with its workload and fatigue.
Would let sponsors justify delayed-specialist-review or unaided comparators by documenting actual turnaround and coverage patterns at deployment sites.
Wants comparisons to capture errors both introduced and prevented, against a real baseline rather than an error-free physician or unintended autonomous use.
Supports risk-proportionate third-party roles but opposes a universal mandate, preserving other routes to independence and avoiding control by a few organizations.
Says the framework applies to multimodal models if it tests cross-modal grounding, study coverage, consistency, reproducibility and sensitivity to configuration changes.
Lists conditions for more postmarket reliance, met by sequestered supervised drafting, and excludes autonomous, direct-to-patient, irreversible or unmonitorable functions.
Accepts the three approaches, adds correction and rejection measures, and lists triggers from model updates and scanner changes to shifts in adoption patterns.
Sees supervisory agents screening for inconsistencies and drift, never as sole safeguard, with independent evaluation and attention to correlated failure.
Keeps the developer accountable while institutions, clinicians, societies, standards bodies and providers contribute under contractual data-sharing and escalation duties.
Scales re-benchmarking to likely effect on clinical behavior: formatting in the quality system, model, prompt or guardrail changes re-evaluated, expanded autonomy reviewed by FDA.
Says a PCCP should define permissible categories, boundaries, prohibited changes, required confirmation and rollback, never an open-ended authorization.
Wants pinning, notice, change logs, audit rights, automatic blocking of unvalidated versions and rollback, disclosing any limits; silent replacement should not be permitted.
Supports master files with listed content if kept current and not treated as authorization, plus alternatives such as contractual disclosure, system cards and version APIs.
Wants agentic evaluation of planning, tool use, permissions, checkpoints, failure handling and rollback, with human confirmation before irreversible actions unless authorized.
Says supervised drafting is not agentic, the label should not decide device status for routing functions, and added action-taking functions are assessed separately.
Keeps patient safety primary but asks FDA to weigh the public-health cost of imposing autonomous-diagnostic evidence burdens on supervised drafting tools.
Argues supervised use yields labeled feedback at clinical volume without added risk, lost if standalone autonomous performance is required before any supervised use.
Says a proportionate path of shadow testing, local validation, limited supervised deployment and staged expansion fits FDA's least-burdensome goal.
Requests guidance stating enforcement discretion for image-analysis functions that only draft private, non-final text for the interpreting specialist under enforced controls.
Lists qualifying conditions: mandatory source-image access, output restricted to the specialist, and clear labelling as unverified AI work product.
Continues the conditions: non-persistence, no automatic finalization, communication or action, physician control, local validation, human factors, monitoring, change control, rollback and exclusions.
Says a separately authorized worklist-prioritization function may share the platform and model, with the combined configuration checked for interactions.
Asks FDA to keep oversight where safeguards lapse, and failing broad discretion, to create a streamlined low-risk pathway with special controls.
Concludes risks should be met through validation, human factors, controls and monitoring, not by treating every image-capable model as an autonomous diagnostician.
Requests a narrowly bounded policy of premarket enforcement discretion for supervised pre-drafting that preserves jurisdiction and patient protections.
